questions.prompt: Which bacterial virulence factor from Module 19 would most directly interfere with complement-driven opsonization?

options.text: Siderophores that pull iron from host cells
Hemolysins that lyse the host's red blood cells
A capsule that blocks phagocyte attachment
Collagenase that digests connective tissue

questions.explanation: Capsules inhibit phagocytosis, the step opsonization is meant to help.

questions.prompt: Killing Gram-negative bacteria releases LPS. How could this make an infection temporarily worse?

options.text: LPS acts as endotoxin and triggers complement and inflammation
LPS blocks interferon from reaching neighboring host cells
LPS lowers body temperature below the bacteria's optimum
LPS destroys C9, so the membrane attack complex can't form

questions.explanation: Links Module 19 endotoxin to Module 21 complement triggers.

questions.prompt: Which statement about complement fragments is FALSE?

options.text: C3a coats bacteria for phagocytosis.
C9 forms the ring-shaped pore.
C3a and C5a act on mast cells.
C5b begins the membrane attack complex.
C3b activates C5.

questions.prompt: A patient's antibodies bind a bacterium and complement is activated. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Only the membrane attack complex can result from antibody activation
Antibody activation prevents inflammation from happening at all
This activation produces interferon instead of the usual outcomes
It's specific activation, but the three outcomes are the same

questions.explanation: Trigger differs; outcomes are the same.

questions.prompt: Why would antiviral drugs that block viral mRNA be valuable, given what you know about interferon?

options.text: They could act like AVPs without making all cells destroy their RNA
They would replace the complement system in fighting bacteria
They would opsonize viruses so macrophages could eat them
They would cause a protective low-grade fever in the patient

questions.explanation: Interferon's weakness is that AVPs destroy RNA broadly.

questions.prompt: Which defense is triggered by the host cell itself detecting that it is making viruses?

options.text: Interferon secretion
Histamine release from a cut
Complement activation by mannose
Opsonization

questions.explanation: The infected cell 'knows its fate is sealed.'

questions.prompt: Order the inflammation events after complement activation.

options.text: WBCs arrive → C3 splits → mast cells burst → fever → swelling and pain
Histamine → C3a binds → C5a binds → pus forms → membrane attack complex
C3a/C5a bind mast cells → histamine → leaky vessels → swelling → WBCs arrive
Interferon → AVPs → histamine → swelling → membrane attack complex

questions.explanation: Same cascade as Module 20 after histamine release.

questions.prompt: A child's fever is 38.5 °C during a bacterial infection, and a parent wants to bring it down immediately. What would the lecture suggest?

options.text: Fever always helps, even when it rises above 45 °C
Fever only works against viruses, so treat it right away
A low-grade fever may be helping, so don't rush to stop it
Fever has no real effect on bacterial enzymes or growth

questions.explanation: Watch for dangerous high fevers instead.

questions.prompt: Which pair of defenses both end with a bacterium being destroyed by enzymes or lysis, but by different routes?

options.text: Histamine (dissolves bacteria) and pyrogens (burst bacterial cells)
Opsonization (digested in a phagolysosome) and MAC (lysed by pores)
Interferon (destroys bacterial RNA) and fever (melts the cell wall)
Mannose (digests bacteria) and LPS (punches pores in bacteria)

questions.explanation: Phagocytosis digests; the MAC bursts the cell.

questions.prompt: Which observation best shows interferon is a LOCAL defense?

options.text: It is made by the liver and stored there until a virus appears
It is stored inside mast cells and released with histamine
It circulates in the blood to every organ after any infection
It is released near the infected cell to protect its neighbors

questions.explanation: Injecting it makes it systemic — which causes side effects.

questions.prompt: Why would recognizing mannose be useless for defending against a virus inside a cell?

options.text: Viruses have no proteins at all for the immune system to find
Mannose is a bacterial sugar, and the virus is hidden inside a cell
Complement can never be activated once a virus is in the body
Mannose is found only on human cells, so it can't mark viruses

questions.prompt: Which list contains only second-line defenses?

options.text: Antibodies, T cells, B cells, memory cells
Complement, interferon, fever, phagocytosis
Tears, saliva, gastric juice, urine
Skin, mucus, lysozyme, sebum, earwax

questions.explanation: First line = barriers/chemicals; third line = antibodies/T cells.

questions.prompt: If a pathogen made a protein that destroyed C3b on its surface, which defense would it mainly avoid?

options.text: Interferon signaling between cells
Mucus clearance by the ciliary escalator
Pyrogen-driven fever responses
Opsonization-enhanced phagocytosis

questions.prompt: Explain why interferon is not used routinely as a drug, even though it is an effective antiviral defense.
questions.explanation: AVPs destroy RNA in general, not just viral RNA. Natural interferon acts locally, but injected interferon circulates everywhere, so cells all over the body make AVPs that destroy their own RNA, causing significant side effects. It may be used only in desperate cases or if it can be delivered locally.

questions.prompt: Compare how a macrophage recognizes a bacterium directly (Module 20) versus with complement's help (Module 21).
questions.explanation: Directly, Toll-like receptors bind common microbial molecules like mannose or LPS. With complement, C3b coats (opsonizes) the bacterium and the macrophage's C3b receptors bind it, making engulfment easier — both are nonspecific unless complement was triggered by antibodies.
